introduction-cattle-vs-pets-revisited.core: Deployments treat Pods as interchangeable cattle. Some workloads aren't: databases need stable identity and storage (StatefulSet), node agents need one Pod per node (DaemonSet), and batch work must run to completion (Job/CronJob). PodDisruptionBudgets protect all of them during voluntary disruptions.

first_principles.problem: A database run as a Deployment loses its data and identity when Pods are rescheduled.
truths: Some must finish, not run forever.

analogy.title: Different staff contracts
analogy.story: Temps (Deployment), named specialists with their own offices (StatefulSet), a guard on every floor (DaemonSet), project contractors (Job).
analogy.breaks: Staff can be retrained; controller types can't be swapped without recreating workloads.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each workload gets the right semantics.

check.q: Which controller runs exactly one Pod per node?

statefulsets-when-identity-matters.core: StatefulSets give each Pod a stable ordinal name (db-0, db-1), a stable DNS name via a headless Service (db-0.db.ns.svc) and its own PersistentVolumeClaim from volumeClaimTemplates that follows it across rescheduling. That suits databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper and other clustered systems needing stable membership.

first_principles.problem: A Kafka broker restarted by a Deployment comes back with a new name and empty disk, confusing the cluster.
truths: Clustered systems track members by identity.
derivation: Remember PVCs **aren't deleted** on scale-down by default.

analogy.title: Named, numbered lockers for team members
analogy.story: Player 3 always gets locker 3 with their kit inside, even after a substitution.
analogy.breaks: Lockers don't move; PVCs bound to zonal disks restrict which nodes a Pod can return to.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: db-0, db-1, db-2 each with their own volume.

check.q: What gives each StatefulSet Pod its own persistent volume?
check.a: volumeClaimTemplates, which create a PVC per Pod ordinal.

statefulsets-ordered-scaling-and-update-.core: By default (OrderedReady), StatefulSets create Pods in order 0→N, each waiting for the previous to be ready, delete them in reverse, and roll updates from the highest ordinal down. Parallel podManagementPolicy speeds independent members. RollingUpdate partitions enable canaries (only ordinals ≥ partition update).

first_principles.problem: A database cluster upgrade updates all replicas at once and loses quorum.
truths: Clustered systems need orderly membership changes.
Updating one member at a time preserves quorum.

analogy.title: Changing guards one at a time
analogy.story: Each new guard is in position before the next one leaves.
analogy.breaks: Guards know when their replacement is ready; readiness probes must express real cluster readiness.

steps.label: Then
steps.detail: Verify db-2, set partition 0 to finish.

code.text:
updateStrategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate: {partition: 2}   # only db-2 gets the new version

check.q: What does a StatefulSet rollingUpdate partition do?
check.a: Only Pods with ordinals greater than or equal to the partition are updated, enabling staged rollouts.

daemonsets-one-pod-per-node.core: A DaemonSet ensures one Pod runs on every node (or every node matching a selector), adding Pods as nodes join and removing them as nodes leave. It's used for node-level agents: log collectors, metrics exporters, CNI plugins, CSI node drivers and security agents, often with tolerations to run on tainted nodes.

first_principles.problem: A log agent deployed with replicas: 10 misses new nodes and doubles up on others.
truths: Some software must run on every node.
derivation: Add **tolerations** for control-plane or special nodes.

analogy.title: A fire extinguisher on every floor
analogy.story: When a floor is added, it gets an extinguisher automatically.
analogy.breaks: Extinguishers sit idle; DaemonSet Pods consume resources on every node, so keep them lean.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every node, including tainted ones, exports metrics.

code.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata: {name: node-exporter}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: node-exporter}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: node-exporter}}
    spec:
      tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]
      hostNetwork: true
      containers: [{name: exporter, image: prom/node-exporter, resources: {requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}}}]

check.q: Why do DaemonSets often include broad tolerations?
check.a: So agents also run on tainted nodes like control-plane or specialised nodes.

jobs-run-to-completion-tasks.core: A Job runs Pods until a specified number complete successfully, retrying failures up to backoffLimit. completions and parallelism control batch size, Indexed completion mode gives each Pod an index for sharded work, activeDeadlineSeconds bounds runtime, and ttlSecondsAfterFinished cleans up. podFailurePolicy can treat certain exit codes as non-retryable.

first_principles.problem: A migration script run as a Deployment restarts forever after finishing.
truths: Failures may be transient or permanent.
Work can be split across Pods.

analogy.title: Hiring contractors to complete a set number of tasks
analogy.story: They retry failed attempts a few times, then report done or give up.
analogy.breaks: Contractors judge failures; Kubernetes needs failure policies to know what not to retry.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 10 shards, 5 at a time, each knows its index.

code.text:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata: {name: shard-process}
spec:
  completions: 10
  parallelism: 5
  completionMode: Indexed
  backoffLimit: 3
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers: [{name: worker, image: proc:1.0, args: ["--shard=$(JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX)"]}]

check.q: What does Indexed completion mode provide?
check.a: Each Pod gets a unique completion index (JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX) to process a specific shard.

cronjobs-scheduled-tasks.core: A CronJob creates Jobs on a cron schedule (with timeZone support). concurrencyPolicy (Allow, Forbid, Replace) controls overlapping runs, startingDeadlineSeconds handles missed schedules, and successful/failedJobsHistoryLimit controls retained history. Jobs should be idempotent because runs can occasionally be duplicated or skipped.

first_principles.problem: A nightly report job runs long, the next run starts on top of it, and both corrupt the output.
truths: Schedules can overlap with long runs.
Controllers can miss or duplicate runs.

analogy.title: An alarm clock that starts a task
analogy.story: If yesterday's task is still running, decide whether to skip, wait or interrupt it.
analogy.breaks: Alarms ring exactly once; CronJobs may occasionally create zero or two Jobs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One run at 02:00 London time, never overlapping.

code.text:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: {name: nightly-report}
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  timeZone: "Europe/London"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 600
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers: [{name: report, image: report:2.1}]

check.a: Skips a new run if the previous Job is still running.

pod-disruption-budgets-protecting-availa.core: A PodDisruptionBudget limits voluntary disruptions (node drains, upgrades, autoscaler scale-down) by requiring minAvailable or capping maxUnavailable Pods for a selector. Eviction requests that would violate it are refused until enough Pods are healthy. It doesn't protect against involuntary failures like node crashes.

first_principles.problem: A node pool upgrade drains nodes simultaneously and takes all replicas of a service down.
truths: Crashes can't be prevented by policy.

analogy.title: A rule that at least two lifeguards are on duty during shift changes
analogy.story: Breaks are allowed, but never all at once.
analogy.breaks: Lifeguard rules can't stop someone fainting; PDBs don't stop involuntary failures.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Drains evict api Pods one at a time.

check.q: Does a PDB protect against a node crashing?
check.a: No; it only limits voluntary disruptions like drains and evictions.
